45.t: Celestin playing endless choruses at the Temple
45.s: He tells of Celestin soloing chorus after chorus while others took down, and that orchestrations were played short.
45.ch: Style and solos in the early bands
45.q: Who would take down? Yeah. Well, if the trumpet player might want to take a solo. Oh, after three ensembles he'd still be strong enough? Man, Celestine looked like he played for hours. Man, Celestine was playing up on the bandstand with us at the temple, I swear to God. He played a tune so long it…

45.t: Ensemble playing, the word jazz, and the arrival of banjo solos
45.s: Early bands played mostly ensemble, about three choruses, with few solos until banjoists like Caffrey came after he returned.
45.ch: Style and solos in the early bands
45.q: Yeah, everybody. Everybody. It's like you're shocking them, everybody playing. Ensemble. That's right. That's right. That's right. That would be the beginning, huh? In the beginning. Then all right, if you had your trumpet player, he wanted to take a solo, well you let him take a solo. You take…

45.t: Whether bands featured trombone and clarinet; everyone laying out for a solo
45.s: Williams says duets were rare and recalls everyone dropping out behind a soloist in Buddy's and Ridgley's bands.
45.ch: Style and solos in the early bands
45.q: Be featured like? Like solos, trombone and clarinet? Well a duet really, the two of the together. Oh no, hardly. Hardly, huh? Hardly. Because you know they didn't know that much about music to play on. Cards you know. They just played on. Well I don't mean cards. I mean tailgate. Yeah. But I know…

418.t: Solo length: a chorus is a story
418.s: In early bands solos were usually one chorus; he thinks a chorus is a story of his imagination and likes two choruses on short pieces and ballads.
418.q: Well no. We played one chorus pieces. They never played -- no, the guys never played a whole lot of choruses, unless they felt like it -- unless the guys felt that they should play another chorus.

418.t: Solo length: a chorus is a story
418.s: In early bands solos were usually one chorus; he thinks a chorus is a story of his imagination.
418.q: Well, no. You'd play maybe one chorus apiece. They never played... Guys didn't play a whole lot of choruses, unless he felt like it or unless the guys felt that they should play another chorus.

722.t: Developing material and guiding soloists: 'a solo is a compositional continuance'
722.s: Rivello develops material first, gives soloists starting guidelines and backgrounds so they stay in the piece.
722.q: What I think about is continuing to develop whatever material is going on before I turn it over to a soloist. And so whether that’s a melodic idea or if then oh well I did this so it was kind of a straightforward thing so maybe I’ll do some kind of a counterpoint that’s an inversion or a retrograde…

722.t: Brookmeyer's advice: wait before giving in to a soloist
722.s: Rowe recalls the advice via Schneider; Rivello confirms it is a Brookmeyer saying.
722.q: That’s a Brookmeyer thing for sure. Yeah. When nothing else can happen, that’s when the first solo should happen. So you should do everything you can until then. Yeah, that’s from Brookmeyer for sure.

508.t: Joey Calderazzo's long failed solo and knowing when to get out
508.s: When Joey joined the band he asked for one more chorus and failed; Branford's advice is to stop when it is not working.
508.ch: Short solos, A Love Supreme and The Tonight Show
508.q: keep playing, and keep…. I remember… (laughs)…when Joey first joined the band. He was playing this tune and he wasn’t playing very well. And he said a…. He believed…. Well, he’s a gambler. He has a gambler’s mentality. “If I play one more chorus, I’m gonna find my way out of this shit.” So he…

508.t: Forty-five-second solos with Sting and the Tonight Show band
508.s: Sting's band forced him to hit it and quit it, which made his later jazz solos more concise.
508.ch: Short solos, A Love Supreme and The Tonight Show
508.q: Yeah, sure. When I was playing in Wynton’s band and I really…. I wasn’t really a jazz musician, I was playing jazz, but I didn’t know what the hell I was doing. But I had learned all these Wayne Shorter solos and we were working out of the mode, the Miles band was kind of our band. So I would play…

234.t: Improvisation: soloists, solo length and cueing
234.s: Johnston asks how Gil inspires soloists. He explains solo lengths, needling from the piano and why he lets players stretch.
234.q: You could name me something that you have in mind or play name me something that I could tell you, but to tell you without hearing what you mean

234.t: Why Gil lets his soloists stretch out
234.s: Gil says that with little work he lets players solo as long as they want, though pieces have a natural length.
234.q: : No, lately I haven't been working very much so whenever I get a chance to work I don't really care about the audience because I'm so hungry to play that I just as soon let the players all play on every number all that they want to because it gives me more chances to be active musically you see.

868.t: Avery and Tillman at Tyler's Beer Garden and solos then and now
868.s: Allen recalls Joe Avery and Wilbur Tillman's band playing lead right through; De De says short solos are the written norm today.

172.s: Ridgley says the whole sixteen bars were thought out ahead, with everyone playing something even during a solo.
172.q: You'd rather have that in mind. For the whole sixteen measures before you even get going? You know, you practice that and you've got it in mind, you know you're going to do it. I see. Well, when I was after you to do that, you see.

182.t: Solos, stomping off and keys in the early bands
182.s: Tom explains there were no solos or singing early on, how he started tunes on violin, the keys F and B flat, and ensemble playing.
182.q: Solos, well, a year old lately they started taking solos. They had all that singing or nothing like that too. Nobody had nothing like that.

248.t: Solos versus ensemble and background in the old bands
248.s: Garland explains how the old bands took choruses in turn with horns backing, and rhythm continuing.
248.ch: Garland on the New Orleans style
248.q: Well, they use more solos now, but in the old days we didn't use the solos as much as we're using now. Yeah. Because I know we played some, I played a lot of solos on my bass violin, you know. Yeah. We didn't do that, you know. But we didn't do much of that. All we done was just give the horns and…

253.t: Building a solo through the registers
253.s: Hall advises starting in the low register and not playing everything in the first chorus.
253.q: You're telling me if you want to build it up, you say, well, I'll start it easy. Work it up. So you start in the low register because you're getting too many guys, you can't play. Yeah. Sometimes it's fun.

36.t: Playing in small groups and the climax of the last chorus
36.s: In a small group, state the melody first, then improvise, then swing the last chorus; drive the out choruses.
36.q: Well, you don't change your style but first you introduce the melody. You get the melody established so that the people can know what you're playing. Then play solos you can improvise, play ad lib, whatever you want to. Then probably on the last chorus then you might, what we call, swing the…

448.t: Bechet's stock variations, one-man band record, playing together at Ryan's
448.s: Bechet passed on his standard variation choruses; Wilber played twin sopranos with him at Ryan's.
448.q: But he showed me all his... He had choruses of variations worked out on certain tunes that he would always play when he played the tunes. They were his specialties, like China Boy, I Know That You Know, The Sheik of Arabi, which he had a whole chorus of variations, which he recorded on the one-man…

2.t: Solos, tourist audiences and Bunk's attitude to playing
2.s: Why a trumpeter never put his horn down, how solos spread, how tourists shape the music, and Bunk's view that playing is not work.
2.q: There was, when Bunk was feeling good, he wouldn't ever put his horn down. In fact, that was the tradition in New Orleans. There might be sometimes, say, at times maybe the clarinet could have been a leader of a band, and he might have sort of featured himself at times. But ordinarily, the trumpet…

664.t: How he plays lead and the last chorus
664.s: He describes ensemble and chorus order, varying the last chorus, and playing alone at home.
664.q: Well, that's a, that's a, uh, quite question and answer. Yeah, I know. I just play the way I feel. I take off in a tempo and that's it. And I try to set that drive until the, the, the piece is kicked out.

300.s: Humphrey contrasts old ensemble playing for long dances with today's solos, which he finds monotonous.
300.q: No, we didn't play. Well, yeah, that's the difference. They didn't play those. No. No. If you did, everybody played right along. The only time a musician would take down in the old days. 537.t: Discussing his solo and the Brownlick
537.s: They listen to a playback of his solo; he explains the Clifford Brown lick and the rhythm section's groove.
537.q: Yeah. That feels good. That’s what music is supposed to feel like. That’s called a Brownlick. That’s where I got that from.

927.t: Sun Ra's challenges: no repeated licks and the Milan standing ovation
927.s: Griffin calls Sun Ra courageous and recalls two lessons: never repeat a lick, and solo alone in Milan until the audience stood.
927.q: Yes. Because he was courageous. He was just like what I was saying about trying stuff. He would try stuff. Although I think he was probably one of the most adventurous or courageous guy out there in the music because he would try stuff. You know. He was always inventing something. And Rahsaan was…

541.t: Trading fours, soloing and listening on the bandstand
541.s: Harper composes solos like Max Roach, bases trading on the previous player, and goes in open to the other musicians.
541.q: I try to mostly go into situations, like I told you, I try to, before I walk out that door I try to make sure look empty my glass so I can come with an empty cup and bring something back. If you’re going to a buffet and you’ve got two sandwiches in your bag, you know what I mean? So I try to make…

421.t: Playing the recorded solo for Miller versus Goodman
421.s: Miller wanted the record solo played live as part of the arrangement; Goodman, by contrast, asked if he liked what he recorded. They discuss Miller's dance-band aims.
421.q: But Glenn was a great experience, a great learning experience. I learned what playing notes properly is right and how to really play by the mark. 1012.t: Oliver Nelson as a soloist and the Stolen Moments solo

660.s: Ries compares freedom in his own gig with limits when playing with the Stones, where his solo on Miss You ends when Mick starts the verse. Al sat in on a Ukrainian polka.

Like there was a period where that accordion player, Al, came up and sat in right. So now we’re incorporating a guy who does polka music…

135.t: Never the same solo twice, unlike solos that became arrangements
135.s: Heath contrasts the MJQ's fresh improvisation with fixed solos like 'Flying Home' and 'Cotton Tail'.
135.ch: Founding the MJQ and bass craft
135.q: Let me tell you, John Lewis set up… he knew, if he did a certain thing, what Jackson would do. They were unbelievable. I played with those people for forty years and I never heard them play the same thing twice. They may have the same vocabulary, but never the same thing in the same place in…

63.q: No, only unless it was like Stardust. That got frozen. More or less you had to play that, because that’s what the audience expected. 377.t: Opening up solos and who takes a chorus
377.s: Basie says the band can open up arrangements any time, nobody plays the same solo twice, and he points to who takes a chorus.
377.q: Well, that would be -- we could be at a rehearsal. Then after we play it a while maybe (inaudible) figure that we want to open it up some more.

26.t: Did the soloists play the same solos as on record?
26.s: Greer says solos were similar not note for note; Jack Hylton again.
26.q: No, similar. Not note for note. Similar. Because they always kept the same -- and a lot of the times we'd make a record and a lot of times when they'd come to the solo it would even be better than on the record. And Duke would say, why didn't you put that on the record? "I never thought of it."…

67.t: Wilbur DeParis giving him freedom to solo, and his improvisation book
67.s: He wrote a book on improvisation, and DeParis gave him free rein to solo, as did European tours.
67.q: I did that, yes, because I wanted to do it. I wanted to express myself some kind of way, so I did it in book form and Wilbur DeParis turned me loose as a soloist. I had free hand and that's what I like. I think he really gave me the more opportunity than anyone.

68.t: Playing record solos versus new ones; Lester never repeated a solo
68.s: Basie bandsmen would extend a hit solo; Lester Young would not repeat solos except on records.

168.t: Keeping a successful recorded solo; It's Got to Be This or That
168.s: Stewart improvised solos differently each time but kept a solo that worked on a hit record, citing It's Got to Be This or That with Goodman.
168.ch: Blanton, Los Angeles and Art Tatum
168.q: -- just about what he was going to do and especially after or rather, I might say, when I took my solos, I would say I would do my solos more or less improvisation, you know, because lots of times I'd never play the same, the solo, my solos the same way twice.

13.t: Repeating the same solo versus improvising
13.s: Common to repeat solos; some never played the same twice.
13.ch: Swing, singers, Ed Fox and recordings
13.q: No, that was pretty common back in those days. But there was some artists that never played the same thing twice. Well, that was their talent.
